content: Cigarette smoking significantly increases the risk of severe adverse effects when using the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring. These risks include heart attacks, blood clots, and strokes. Women over the age of 35 and those who smoke heavily (15 or more cigarettes per day) are at an even higher risk. If you are using this contraceptive ring, you should not smoke. The etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring is a prescription medication used to prevent pregnancy. It belongs to a class of drugs known as combination hormonal contraceptives. Etonogestrel is a synthetic progestin, and ethinyl estradiol is a synthetic estrogen. This contraceptive works by inhibiting ovulation, which is the release of an egg from the ovaries. Additionally, it alters the uterine lining to prevent implantation of a fertilized egg and thickens cervical mucus to block sperm from entering the uterus. While this method is highly effective in preventing pregnancy, it does not protect against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. The contraceptive ring is a flexible device that is inserted into the vagina. It is typically left in place for three weeks, followed by a one-week break, during which a new ring is inserted. It is essential to follow the instructions provided by your healthcare provider or pharmacist carefully. Never use more than one ring at a time, and always adhere to the schedule provided by your doctor. The ring should be inserted and removed on the same day of the week and at approximately the same time each cycle. Your menstrual period will likely begin two to three days after removing the ring and may continue during the one-week break. Even if you are still bleeding, you must insert a new ring at the end of the one-week interval on the same day and time as usual. Your doctor will provide specific instructions on when to insert your first contraceptive ring, depending on whether you were previously using another form of birth control, were not using contraception, or recently experienced childbirth, an abortion, or a miscarriage. In some cases, you may need to use an additional method of contraception, such as condoms or spermicides, for the first seven days of using the ring. Note that diaphragms should not be used concurrently with the contraceptive ring. The ring does not need to be positioned in a specific way within the vagina to be effective, but it should be placed as far back as possible for comfort and to reduce the likelihood of it slipping out. The ring cannot pass beyond the cervix, so it will not become lost inside the body. However, it may occasionally slip out during activities such as tampon removal, bowel movements, or if it was not inserted correctly. If the ring slips out, rinse it with cool or lukewarm water (not hot) and reinsert it as soon as possible. If the ring is lost, replace it with a new one and remove it according to the original schedule. If the ring is out of the vagina for more than three hours, you must use a backup contraceptive method for seven consecutive days after reinserting the ring. To insert the contraceptive ring: 1. Wash and dry your hands thoroughly. 2. Remove the ring from its foil pouch, keeping the pouch for disposal later. 3. Choose a comfortable position, such as lying on your back with knees bent, squatting, or standing with one leg elevated. 4. Squeeze the ring between your thumb and index finger to compress it. 5. Gently push the folded ring into your vagina as far as it will comfortably go. 6. If you feel discomfort, push the ring further back using your index finger. 7. Wash your hands again after insertion. To remove the ring: 1. Hook your index finger under the front rim or grasp the rim between your index and middle fingers and pull it out. 2. Place the used ring in the foil pouch and dispose of it in a trash can, keeping it out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush the ring down the toilet. 3. Wash your hands after removal. 4. Wait one week before inserting a new ring, following the same steps. This medication may be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Before using the etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring, inform your doctor if you are allergic to any of its components or other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription drugs, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, as some may interact with the contraceptive ring. Medications such as certain antibiotics, antifungals, seizure medications, and herbal products like St. John’s wort may reduce the effectiveness of the ring, necessitating the use of backup contraception. Notify your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you are undergoing surgery or wearing contact lenses, inform your healthcare provider, as the ring may affect these situations. Discuss with your doctor whether it is safe to consume grapefruit juice while using this medication. If you forget to insert a new ring after the one-week break, you may not be protected against pregnancy. Insert a new ring as soon as you remember and use a backup contraceptive method for seven consecutive days. If you forget to remove the ring on time but remember within one week, remove it immediately, wait one week, and insert a new ring. If more than one week has passed, check for pregnancy before continuing use. The contraceptive ring may cause side effects. Common but less severe side effects include vaginal irritation, discharge, spotting, headaches, nausea, weight changes, breast tenderness, acne, and changes in sexual desire. Severe side effects, though rare, include symptoms such as leg pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headaches, vision changes, yellowing of the skin or eyes, depression, or abdominal pain. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any severe symptoms. The ring may increase the risk of liver tumors, breast or liver cancer, heart attacks, strokes, or blood clots. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Store the medication in its original packaging at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Keep it out of reach of children. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services. Symptoms of overdose may include nausea, vomiting, or irregular vaginal bleeding. Inform laboratory personnel that you are using this medication before undergoing any tests. Do not share this medication with others. If you have questions, consult your pharmacist. The brand name for this medication is NuvaRing®.
